Base decisions: low + wide (low center of gravity, more accurate turns; tradeoff = harder in tight spaces). Reinforced the base to make it rigid. Discussed color sensors — decided to use no sensors because the compact base had no room for one.
Finished the attachment for the Forest Elder (M12) and did the programming for it.
Did the programming for Drone Survey (M01) — our first mission program!

Our solution idea: a camera to put in the forest. It has an AI camera to tag animals, solar panels and batteries so it can charge in the sun, and it sends the images to a website we built. Now gathering materials.
Fynn programmed mission 14 (Seeds of Renewal) and got 5/5 in the tests. Our first test session!
Adeline finished programming mission 15 (Biocentric Architecture) and mission 12 (Forest Elder).
Nolan programmed missions 2 and 3 (Exploding Seeds + Flip the Rock) and got 5/5 in his tests.
Weston worked on building the attachments for the tree mission.

Picked Option B: build the forest camera on our own Raspberry Pi 4, running 24/7 on solar. We already have the Raspberry Pi 4, an m5cam module, and a microSD card. Next: buy a camera, motion sensor, night light, solar panel, battery, and a waterproof box.

Coach CJ helped research a cheaper, low-power camera (Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 Sense) instead of the Raspberry Pi 4. It sleeps between animals and needs a much smaller solar panel, but it needs night vision added, and the animal tagging would happen later on a bigger computer. Deciding between XIAO only, Pi 4 only, or both together.

We will use the Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense board for the forest camera. It has Wi-Fi built in. Our Raspberry Pi 4 will connect to it over Wi-Fi to get the pictures. Next: test how far the Wi-Fi reaches in the forest.

Our coach helped us plan two cameras. Camera 1 plugs into power behind our house with a view of the forest, for testing and live streaming over Wi-Fi. Camera 2 goes in the forest in solar mode and turns on and off with movement. A switch picks "always on mode" or "solar mode": to collect pictures we walk up, flip it to always on so the Wi-Fi connects, download, then switch back. Both use USB-C power. Parts list made.

We met our first expert, Nate Ragan from Arizona Game and Fish. There are about 300 animal strikes in a year on I-17, and the I-17 wildlife bridge is supposed to reduce collisions by 90%. Baby animals follow their mom across. He said not to live stream, to use AI to blur out people, and that cameras over a wide area work best. We need ADOT's permission to use the bridge; if that doesn't work out, we could watch the squirrel nest.

We brought 5 questions for Nate Ragan (Game and Fish): how many animal crashes happen in Flagstaff, our blinking warning light idea, live stream cameras, how long animals take to trust a new bridge, and how they will count animals on the new I-17 overpass at Willard Springs. New idea: the camera makes a blinking light to warn drivers about an animal crossing (Nate said it has been done before).

We bought the parts for our camera. Solar box: 6V 3W solar panel, Waveshare Solar Power Manager (D), two 2600 mAh 18650 batteries (still shipping). Camera box: Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, AM312 motion sensors, DS3231 clock modules. The solar box and the camera box are two different options: the camera gets USB-C power from a phone charger, or from the solar box if there is no power nearby. We are starting by wiring the camera box while the batteries are delayed.

Fynn and Isla tested all of the missions and timed them. Mission 1 = 12 sec, missions 4+5 = 17 sec, mission 12 = 7 sec, missions 13+12 = 17 sec, missions 6+7+11 = 17 sec. Still to fix: missions 2+3 (needs help), 8+9 and 10+14 (needs work), mission 15 (fix yellow arm).

Nolan researched whether wildlife crossings work and found 9 sources (KJZZ, LA Times, WWF, Leave No Trace and more). Almost all say crossings cut crashes 70–96%, but only if animals actually use them, and someone has to check: in Nepal they proved it with camera traps. That is what our camera on the I-17 Willard Springs bridge would do.

experts.name: Nate Ragan
experts.feedback: Don't live stream: that prevents bad stuff. Use AI to edit the video or blur out any people. Cameras over a wide area work best. Get our own data, and ask ADOT before using the I-17 wildlife bridge.
experts.improvement: Still deciding: live stream or not, the wildlife bridge or the squirrel nest (backup), one camera or several.

research.note: Pi 4 uses 3–5 W all the time and takes ~30 s to start. A Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 Sense camera board sleeps between animals and runs on a small 6 V solar panel + one 18650 battery. Missing: night vision, species tagging.

research.source: Nate Ragan, Arizona Game and Fish — interview
research.note: ~300 animal strikes a year on I-17; the I-17 wildlife bridge should cut collisions 90%. Game and Fish use GPS collars, thermal goggles, satellite cameras and drones, not much AI.

research.source: KJZZ radio — This I-17 Willard Springs Wildlife Overpass near Flagstaff allows animals to safely cross highway
research.note: Our bridge! ADOT is building it south of Flagstaff with money from a federal pilot program. Mostly to stop elk crashes: Game and Fish (Jeff Gagnon) collared elk starting around 2007 to find where they cross. Fences steer animals to the bridge, and plants on the bridge make it feel natural. Some crossings went from about 400 crashes a year to zero; elk take time to learn, and crashes drop about 40% a year. Even shy pronghorn use bridges.

research.source: Los Angeles Times — Wildlife crossings aren't enough to curb roadkill hot spots, researchers say
research.note: UC Davis: cars kill about 780 mountain lions (18%) and 44,000 mule deer a year in California. Crossings need long fences too: "just building a crossing doesn't mean wildlife will use it." Best fence: at least 8 ft tall, fine mesh at the bottom, overhang on top. Crossings + fencing can cut big-animal crashes by more than 80% (Pew).

research.source: WWF — Wildlife Crossings Reduce Collisions and Save Lives
research.note: US cars hit large animals 1–2 million times a year: $8 billion+ in costs and 200 people killed. Banff (6 bridges + 38 underpasses) cut crashes 80%. Montana Hwy 93: 42 crossings, 22,000+ animals a year, crashes down 70%+. Nepal used camera traps to prove 13 species used 4 underpasses (like our camera idea!).

research.source: Think Wildlife Foundation — How effective are wildlife crossings?
research.note: Banff's 44 crossings cut big-animal crashes 80%+. Netherlands: roadkill down 96% for some species. A study of 89 crossings found more animals cross where structures are. Crossings only work if they are in the right place, kept clear, and the right size for the animal.

research.source: Leave No Trace — Up, Under and Across: How Do Wildlife Cross a Road?
research.note: Kinds of crossings: bridge, underpass, tunnel, culvert, canopy bridge. First US wildlife bridge: Utah, 1975. Arizona is one of the crash hot-spot states with crossings. Fits Leave No Trace Principle #6, Respect Wildlife.

research.source: All That's Interesting — Wildlife Crossings: 25 Stunning Animal Bridges From Around The World
research.note: Over a million animals are killed by cars every day (estimate). Expert Ben Goldfarb: crossings + fences cut crashes "by 90 percent or so." Banff: 150,000+ animals used its crossings 1996–2016. Arizona: about 20 wildlife bridges since 2000 (page gives no source).

research.source: Sigma Earth — Can Wildlife Bridge Truly Make A Difference In Conserving Endangered Species?
research.note: Bridges + fences cut deer, bear and mountain lion roadkill by about 90%. Netherlands: 600+ green bridges. Not every animal uses them (shy or night animals may not), so each design has to fit its animals. Bridges need upkeep and checking after they're built.

research.source: Gokce Capital — Wildlife Crossings: 11 Things (2026) You Have to Know
research.note: Banff: crashes down 80–90% (about 100 a year before, fewer than 6 now), but animals can take years to start using a crossing. A crossing costs $500,000 to $6 million; underpasses cost less. US Wildlife Crossings Pilot Program (2021): $350 million in grants over 5 years.

research.source: ResearchGate — Twenty years of research, do animals use wildlife crossings?

tradeoffs.question: Low and wide, or tall and narrow?
tradeoffs.options: Low + wide base vs taller, narrower base
tradeoffs.why: Low center of gravity so it doesn't tip. Wide wheelbase makes turns more accurate. Tradeoff we accepted: harder to move in tight spaces on the field.

tradeoffs.question: Reinforce the base or keep it light?
tradeoffs.why: Made the base more rigid so it doesn't flex or twist — attachments line up the same way every run.

tradeoffs.question: Color sensors, or no sensors?
tradeoffs.options: Color sensors (line / color detection) vs none
tradeoffs.why: The base is so compact there was no room left for a sensor. Tradeoff we accepted: no line or color detection — the robot navigates by wheel rotations and turns alone.

tradeoffs.question: One robot base, or three identical copies?
tradeoffs.options: One base everyone shares vs three matching bases
tradeoffs.why: (students: write why here — more attachments tested at once? a spare if one breaks?)

tradeoffs.question: One attachment for Missions 2 + 3, or two separate ones?
tradeoffs.options: Adeline's Mission 2 attachment vs Nolan's combined 2 + 3 attachment
tradeoffs.why: Test both, then pick — and write down why. That's exactly what judges want to see.
